chunks: Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id, from al-Hasan, from Zur'ah, from Sama'ah, who said:

I asked him about salat (prayer) by night and day when neither the sun nor the moon nor the stars can be seen. He said: You exert your judgment and deliberately face the qiblah to the best of your ability.

Thus, the proper way regarding these reports is that we understand them as applying to a state of necessity in which a person is unable to perform salat (prayer) toward four directions. In that case, informed estimation suffices for him; but if he is able, then he must perform salat (prayer) toward four directions.

key_terms.أَرْبَعِ جِهَاتٍ: four directions, the precautionary method when one is able
key_terms.التَّحَرِّي: careful estimation or informed determination when certainty is unavailable
key_terms.الشَّمْسُ: the sun, a natural sign used to determine direction
key_terms.الصَّلَاةِ: salat (prayer), the ritual prayer whose valid direction is being discussed
key_terms.الضَّرُورَةِ: necessity, the constraining circumstance affecting the ruling
key_terms.النُّجُومُ: the stars, celestial markers for locating the qiblah
key_terms.الْقِبْلَةَ: the qiblah, the direction one must face in salat (prayer)
key_terms.جُهْدَكَ: to the best of your ability, indicating maximal effort

ai.seo_question: What should a person do for qiblah direction if the sun, moon, and stars are not visible?
ai.summary: This report addresses the ruling for determining the qiblah when celestial signs are not visible. It states that one should exert personal judgment to face the qiblah, while the compiler explains that this applies in necessity; otherwise, if possible, one should pray toward four directions.
